T1.claim: Consumers will adopt Jotun coatings for home DIY projects if they perceive them as premium, durable marine-grade products that offer superior protection and longer lifespan compared to standard paints.
T1.who_benefits: DIY homeowners seeking high-performance protective coatings for exterior surfaces (e.g., siding, garage doors).
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers view marine coatings as a premium, specialized solution, they will be willing to pay a premium price and choose Jotun over generic paints, especially for high-value assets.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Jotun can charge premium prices for marine-grade coatings and sell under its own brand, capturing higher margins and building brand equity in the consumer DIY segment.
assumptions: Consumers differentiate marine coatings from standard paints.
Performance claims (durability, protection) are credible and can be communicated effectively.
Jotun can reach DIY consumers through existing distribution (e.g., hardware stores, online) without major new channels.
predictions: In a test offering marine-grade DIY coating at a 20% price premium compared to standard paint, purchase intent will be at least 15% higher among DIY homeowners.
Willingness to pay will be positively correlated with perceived protection benefits (e.g., longer lifespan, resistance to weathering).
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt Jotun coatings for home DIY projects if they perceive them as premium, durable marine-grade products that offer superior protection and longer lifespan compared to standard paints.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt Jotun coatings for home DIY projects if they perceive them as a convenient, ready-to-use solution that requires no special preparation or expertise, reducing purchase friction compared to professional-grade coatings.
T2.who_benefits: DIY homeowners who value ease of use and quick application, especially those with limited time or DIY experience.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers view marine coatings as a plug-and-play product that can be applied directly from the can without priming or special tools, they will choose Jotun over more complex professional coatings, because the lower barrier to entry.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Jotun can price at a modest premium for convenience, sell through existing retail channels (hardware stores, online), and capture volume sales driven by ease of use, generating incremental revenue without major new distribution.
assumptions: Consumers associate marine coatings with professional-grade quality but also seek simplicity.
Jotun can formulate a product that meets marine standards while being easy to apply.
Retail partners will stock a convenient DIY coating because it increases shelf space utilization.
predictions: In a test offering a marine-grade DIY coating that requires no priming or special tools at a 10% price premium compared to standard paint, purchase intent will be at least 12% higher among DIY homeowners.
Willingness to pay will be inversely related to perceived complexity of application (e.g., "no prep" vs. "requires primer").

X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 500 DIY homeowners in Scandinavia (Norway, Sweden, Denmark) recruited via panel, balanced for age, gender, and home ownership status.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and WTP premium (percentage above standard paint price).

prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent for marine-grade coating will be at least 15% higher than for standard paint, and WTP premium will be inversely correlated with perceived complexity of application (e.g., "no prep" vs. "requires primer").

final.recommendation: Do not launch a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Instead, run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness-to-pay for marine-grade DIY coating versus standard paint. If the test meets the decision rule (purchase intent ≥15% higher and WTP premium ≥10%), proceed to a limited launch (e.g., pilot in Jotun Multicolor Centers). If not, abandon consumer expansion.
final.target_customer: DIY homeowners in Scandinavia (Norway, Sweden, Denmark) seeking high-performance protective coatings for exterior surfaces.
final.value_proposition: A marine-grade DIY coating that offers superior durability, protection, and longer lifespan compared to standard paints, sold under the Jotun brand through existing retail channels (hardware stores, online).
final.next_action: Execute the Consumer Preference Test (X1) within the 12‑week timeline and €15,000 budget, using the proposed methodology.
final.uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain because there is no direct evidence from public sources that consumers perceive marine coatings as premium or convenient, nor that they would pay a premium for these attributes.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for marine-grade coating is at least 15% higher than for standard paint and the average willingness-to-pay premium is at least 10%, indicating demand for a differentiated proposition.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence that a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, built on Jotun’s marine and protective coatings technology, would generate demand and justify the investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources available up to mid-2024; no internal company data.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home DIY, automotive, outdoor gear) using Jotun’s marine/protective coatings.

T1.who_benefits: Jotun gains higher margins and brand loyalty from premium consumer purchases.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers shift from generic automotive coatings to Jotun, they switch from price‑sensitive purchases to value‑based buying, motivated by evidence of superior performance.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Jotun can charge a premium price for its coatings and sell through specialty retailers or online channels, capturing the higher margin.
assumptions: Consumers in target markets (e.g., Scandinavia, Western Europe) have sufficient information about Jotun’s marine/protective coatings.
Automotive DIY buyers are willing to pay a premium for durability.
Jotun can reach these consumers through existing distribution (e.g., Jotun Multicolor Centers, online store).
predictions: If a test offers Jotun coatings at a 20% price premium compared to generic competitors, purchase intent will be at least 15% higher among DIY automotive users.
Surveyed consumers will cite durability and long‑lasting protection as primary reasons for choosing Jotun over cheaper alternatives.

Participants indicate their maximum price they would pay for each version (EUR) and their likelihood to purchase (1‑10).
X1.sample: 500 DIY homeowners in Scandinavia (Norway, Sweden, Denmark) recruited via panel, balanced for age, gender, and home ownership status.
X1.measure: Average willingness-to-pay (WTP) difference between premium and eco-friendly versions (EUR). Secondary measures: purchase intent (percentage indicating "very likely" to buy) and willingness to switch from current brand.

X1.decision_rule: If the premium version’s average WTP exceeds the eco-friendly version’s by ≥ 10% (EUR 35 vs EUR 32), proceed with premium positioning. If the difference is <10%, both positioning could be viable, but further

revisions.reason: Simulated result SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer willingness to pay for premium or eco-friendly coatings. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Instead, conduct the proposed willingness-to-pay survey (Test X1) to empirically compare premium vs. eco-friendly positioning before any investment. The survey will provide real evidence on consumer willingness to pay, which is the critical factor for justifying a differentiated proposition.
final.target_customer: DIY homeowners in Scandinavia (Norway, Sweden, Denmark) seeking high-performance, durable finishes for home projects.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated Jotun coating line that emphasizes premium performance, durability, and design, positioned as a premium brand for discerning consumers willing to pay for superior quality.
final.next_action: Run the willingness-to-pay survey (Test X1) with 500 DIY homeowners, measure average willingness-to-pay differences, and apply the decision rule to determine whether to proceed with premium positioning, eco-friendly positioning, or no
final.uncertainty: Both premium (T1) and eco-friendly (T2) positioning remain uncertain due to lack of direct consumer willingness-to-pay data. The survey will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the survey shows the eco-friendly version’s average willingness-to-pay exceeds the premium version’s by ≥ 10%, we would shift focus to eco-friendly positioning.
If the premium version’s average willingness-to-pay exceeds the eco-friendly version’s by ≥ 10%, we would proceed with premium positioning.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence that a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, built on Jotun’s marine and protective coatings technology, would generate demand and justify the investment.
constraints: Limited to public sources available up to mid-2024; no internal company data.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home DIY, automotive, outdoor gear) using Jotun’s marine/protective coatings.

3) Maintain current B2B focus and not pursue consumer expansion (no expansion).

T1.who_benefits: DIY homeowners seeking high-performance protective coatings for exterior surfaces (e.g., siding, garage doors).
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers view marine coatings as a premium, specialized solution, they will be willing to pay a premium price and choose Jotun over generic paints, especially for high-value assets.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Jotun can charge premium prices for marine-grade coatings and sell under its own brand, capturing higher margins and building brand equity in the consumer DIY segment.
assumptions: Consumers research product performance before purchase.
Price sensitivity is lower for premium, performance-driven products.
Jotun can communicate marine-grade benefits effectively to DIY consumers.
predictions: DIY consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for marine-grade coatings compared to standard paints.
Surveyed DIY buyers will rank Jotun higher than competitors on durability and protection attributes.
Sales of Jotun decorative coatings will grow faster in regions with strong DIY participation.

T2.how_value_is_captured: Jotun can bundle decorative and protective coatings into a single kit, capture higher margins from bundled sales, and potentially expand into adjacent home improvement categories without major product redesign.
assumptions: DIY consumers prioritize ease of use over price sensitivity for a single product.
Jotun can effectively communicate the "all-in-one" benefit to DIY buyers.
The bundled kit can be sold through existing Jotun Multicolor Centers and online channels.
predictions: DIY consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 10% more for a bundled kit compared to buying separate paints.
Surveyed DIY buyers will rank Jotun higher than competitors on "ease of use" and "one-stop shopping".
Sales of Jotun decorative coatings will increase in regions where DIY participation is driven by convenience.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available in 1993.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Tanita’s existing B2B clinic/health club product and its unknown consumer reach.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, and feasibility of consumer adoption.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual home users with a specific use case (e.g., weight management, fitness tracking).
2) Expand the existing clinic/health club product into a broader B2B market (e.g., corporate wellness programs, senior centers).
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus on existing B2B segments.
4) License the bioelectrical impedance technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.

T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita would sell the device directly to consumers at a premium price, capturing margin through retail distribution.

Consumers are willing to invest in home health monitoring devices.
Price sensitivity is manageable for target segment.

X1.name: Consumer Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Home Body-Fat Analyzer
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are recruited via a panel of adults aged 25-55 in Japan (reflecting 1993 demographic). They are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: (A) receive a description of a home body-fat analyzer with a price of ¥15,000 (approx. $130 in 1993 dollars) and are asked if they would purchase it; (B) receive the same description plus a statement that insurance would reimburse the cost. The primary outcome is the proportion of participants who indicate intent to purchase in each condition. Secondary
X1.sample: 400 participants (200 per condition) to detect a 10 percentage point difference with 80% power and a 5% significance level.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy" vs. "Would not buy") and willingness to pay (open-ended).

prediction_by_theory.T1: In condition A (no insurance), at least 30% of participants will indicate intent to purchase at ¥15,000.
prediction_by_theory.T2: In condition B (insurance coverage), at least 40% of participants will indicate intent to purchase at ¥15,000.

final.value_proposition: A stand‑alone home body‑fat analyzer that provides accurate, easy‑to‑use measurement of body composition, sold at a premium price of ¥15,000 (approx. $130 in 1993).

X1.name: Consumer Purchase Intent Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Recruit 400 health‑conscious adults in Japan (200 per group). Randomly assign participants to one of two groups: Group A receives a product description emphasizing home use, premium accuracy, and a 20% price premium over clinic models; Group B receives a product description emphasizing insurance subsidy, volume pricing, and a 15% discount off clinic models. Both descriptions include a link to a landing page where participants can register interest (email) and
X1.sample: 400 respondents (200 per group)
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured by registration email count within 12 weeks

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will generate at least 15% more email registrations than Group B (i.e., a 15% difference in registration rates).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will generate at least 15% more email registrations than Group A (i.e., a 15% difference in registration rates).

X1.decision_rule: If Group A registrations exceed Group B by ≥15%, conclude T1 is more likely. If Group B registrations exceed Group A by ≥15%, conclude T2 is more likely. If the difference is <15%, both theories remain uncertain.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Purchase Intent Test (X1) to measure demand for a home body-fat analyzer priced at a premium. If the test shows a ≥15% registration advantage for the premium messaging, proceed to develop a differentiated home use proposition; otherwise, maintain the existing B2B focus.
final.target_customer: Health‑conscious adults in Japan who are willing to pay a premium for accurate body‑fat tracking and are not reliant on insurance coverage.
final.value_proposition: A stand‑on bioelectrical impedance body‑fat analyzer marketed as a reliable, easy‑to‑use home health tool, priced at a 20% premium over clinic models, offering premium accuracy and convenience.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Purchase Intent Test (X1) within 12 weeks, targeting 400 health‑conscious adults in Japan with two messaging groups. Measure email registration rates and compare premium versus insurance‑subsidy messaging.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand and willingness to pay for a home device. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows a ≥15% advantage for the insurance‑subsidy messaging, indicating T2 is more likely, the recommendation would shift to pursue a volume‑based B2B model with insurer reimbursement.
If the test shows no significant difference or a disadvantage for either messaging, the recommendation would remain unchanged and no consumer expansion would be pursued.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available in 1993.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Tanita’s existing B2B clinic/health club product and its unknown consumer reach.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, and feasibility of consumer adoption.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual home users with a specific use case (e.g., weight management, fitness tracking).
2) Expand the existing clinic/health club product into a broader B2B market (e.g., corporate wellness programs, senior centers).
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus on existing B2B segments.
4) License the bioelectrical impedance technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.

X1.name: Consumer vs Corporate Purchase Intent Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: (A) Health‑conscious consumers (n=200) and (B) Corporate wellness program managers (n=200). Each participant views a product description of a home body‑fat analyzer priced at €180 (just below the €200 threshold). They are asked: "Would you purchase this device for personal use?" (binary yes/no). Additionally, for corporate group, they are asked: "Would you place an order for 500 devices for your wellness program?" (binary yes/no).
X1.sample: 400 adults: 200 health‑conscious consumers recruited via consumer panels, 200 corporate wellness managers recruited via professional networks.
X1.measure: Purchase intent for consumers (percentage saying yes) and corporate order intent (percentage saying yes).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Consumer purchase intent ≥ 30% (supports the idea that health‑conscious consumers will adopt the device). Corporate order intent ≤ 10% (supports the idea that corporate wellness programs will adopt the device).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Consumer purchase intent ≤ 20% (supports the idea that corporate buyers will drive bulk purchases). Corporate order intent ≥ 30% (supports the idea that corporate wellness programs will adopt the device).

X1.decision_rule: If consumer purchase intent ≥ 30% and corporate order intent ≤ 10% → favor T1. If consumer purchase intent ≤ 20% and corporate order intent ≥ 30% → favor T2. If neither condition is met, the evidence is insufficient to justify investment.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer demand, corporate adoption, or medical evidence linking body fat to health outcomes. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

tool_result.question: It is 1993. Should Tanita develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser for clinics and health clubs? What evidence would justify that investment?
tool_result.brief: Tanita is a Tokyo maker of weighing instruments, including commercial scales, that has launched a stand-on body-fat analyser using bioelectrical impedance for clinics and health clubs. You have not been told how far it already reaches individual buyers, so find out. You are an outside analyst working only from public sources. This company has not asked this question, has not been contacted, and nothing here describes its intentions. Many sources were written after the decision date: reason only from what was knowable on that date, and do not use what you may know about later events. Financial data is not in the dossier, so say what you could not find. Product redesign, a different route to buyers, a different customer group and no expansion are all open. The test budget of 20000 euros and the 12-week limit are analyst assumptions for this exercise, not company figures.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed Consumer Willingness to Pay Survey (test X1) to measure willingness to pay €150 and willingness to accept insurance subsidy. If the survey meets the decision thresholds (>=40% at €150 without subsidy and >=30% at €150 with subsidy), proceed to develop a consumer proposition targeting individual home users. Otherwise, maintain the B2B/B2C

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available in 1993.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Tanita’s existing B2B clinic/health club product and its unknown consumer reach.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, and feasibility of consumer adoption.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual home users for personal health monitoring.
2) Expand the existing clinic/health club product line without a new consumer proposition (status quo).
3) Pursue a different route to market or customer group, such as partnering with retailers or targeting corporate wellness programs.
4) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus on existing B2B customers.

T1.claim: Health-conscious consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if they perceive it as a convenient, accurate way to monitor their weight and body composition, and are willing to pay a premium for a trusted brand.
T1.who_benefits: Individual consumers seeking personal health data and a convenient tool.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Survey (Test X1) to measure willingness to pay for a health-focused home body-fat analyzer before committing resources. If the survey shows a premium of at least 15% for the health description, proceed with a health-focused consumer proposition; otherwise, consider other options or no expansion.

frame.objective: Determine whether Tanita should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its stand-on bioelectrical impedance body-fat analyser, leveraging evidence available in 1993.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must consider Tanita’s existing B2B clinic/health club product and its unknown consumer reach.
Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, competitive landscape, and feasibility of consumer adoption.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual home users with a specific use case (e.g., weight management, fitness tracking).
2) Expand the existing clinic/health club product into a broader B2B market (e.g., corporate wellness programs, senior centers).
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus on existing B2B segments.
4) License the bioelectrical impedance technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.

T1.claim: Health‑conscious consumers will adopt a home body‑fat analyzer if they perceive it as a reliable, easy‑to‑use tool for weight management, and they are willing to pay a premium for accuracy.
T1.who_benefits: Consumers seeking to monitor body composition for health and weight control; Tanita would benefit by capturing premium pricing and repeat purchases of accessories.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing public awareness of body‑fat percentage as a health indicator (e.g., heart disease, diabetes) combined with the convenience of a stand‑on device will motivate individuals to purchase a home analyzer.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Tanita would sell the device at a higher price point and potentially offer consumables (e.g., measurement strips) or subscription services for data tracking.
assumptions: Consumers trust bioelectrical impedance as a valid method for body‑fat measurement.
There is sufficient disposable income among target consumers to afford a premium home scale.
Marketing can effectively communicate the health benefits and ease of use.
predictions: Surveyed consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 15% above the price of standard bathroom scales for a body‑fat analyzer.
Pilot sales of a consumer‑branded home model will exceed 5,000 units within 12 weeks if positioned as a health tool.
T1.first_claim: Health‑conscious consumers will adopt a home body‑fat analyzer if they perceive it as a reliable, easy‑to‑use tool for weight management, and they are willing to pay a premium for accuracy.

T2.claim: Fitness‑oriented consumers will adopt a home body‑fat analyzer if they view it as a performance‑enhancing tool that provides actionable data for training and competition, and they are willing to pay a premium for real‑time feedback.
T2.who_benefits: Consumers who engage in regular exercise and track performance; Tanita would benefit by selling devices at premium prices and offering subscription services for data analysis.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Growing popularity of fitness culture and the desire for measurable, immediate feedback on training effectiveness will motivate consumers to purchase a home device that provides body‑fat and performance metrics.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Tanita would sell the device at a higher price point and offer optional subscription services for data visualization, coaching insights, or integration with fitness apps.
assumptions: Consumers trust bioelectrical impedance as a valid method for measuring body composition.
There is a segment of consumers willing to invest in fitness technology beyond basic equipment.
Marketing can highlight the device’s real‑time performance data as a competitive advantage.
predictions: Surveyed fitness consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% above the price of standard bathroom scales for a device that provides body‑fat and performance metrics.
Pilot sales of a fitness‑focused home model will exceed 3,000 units within 12 weeks if positioned as a training tool.

X1.sample: 500 adults aged 18-55, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and region. Participants must have used a fitness tracker or weight-loss program in the past year.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about ACR’s current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer distress beacons.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, competitive landscape, and value capture for ACR.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency distress beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/B2G product line into new segments (e.g., commercial marine, personal safety) without a new consumer proposition.
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus resources on existing markets.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.
5) Form a partnership with outdoor/recreational brands to co‑brand a consumer distress beacon, leveraging existing distribution channels.

Participants view a product description of the 406 MHz distress beacon, indicating it is "designed for outdoor recreation enthusiasts to provide reliable distress signaling in remote environments." They are asked: "Would you purchase this beacon for personal outdoor recreation use?" (yes/no). In a separate random half, the same product description is modified to state: "Designed for emergency responders and search and rescue teams to pinpoint distress signals globally." They are asked: "Would you purchase this beacon for professional use?" (yes/no).
X1.sample: 500 participants: 250 outdoor recreation enthusiasts (recruited via hiking forums and outdoor retailers) and 250 emergency services personnel (recruited via professional associations).

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency distress beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/B2G product line into new segments (e.g., commercial marine, personal safety) without a new consumer proposition.
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus resources on existing markets.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.

2) Expand the existing B2B/B2G product line into new segments (e.g., commercial marine, personal safety) without a new consumer proposition.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about ACR’s current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer distress beacons.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, competitive landscape, and value capture for ACR.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency distress beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/B2G product line into new segments (e.g., commercial marine, personal safety) without a new consumer proposition.
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus resources on existing markets.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.
5) Form a partnership with outdoor/recreational brands to co‑brand a consumer distress beacon, leveraging existing distribution channels.

T1.claim: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt a differentiated consumer distress beacon because they value safety in remote environments and are willing to pay a premium for a device that provides reliable distress signaling.
T1.who_benefits: Outdoor recreation participants (hikers, paddlers, climbers) who engage in activities where emergency response is limited.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Legalization of 406 MHz PLBs in the US (2002) and increased media coverage of successful rescues create a perceived safety necessity; these users already carry emergency gear and are motivated by personal safety.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell a premium-priced, easy-to-use distress beacon directly to consumers through outdoor retailers and online channels, capturing higher margins than bulk B2B sales.
assumptions: Legalization and media coverage will sustain consumer awareness and demand.
Consumers will prioritize safety over cost in a life-threatening situation.
Distribution channels (outdoor retailers, online) can reach the target audience.
predictions: A survey of outdoor recreation participants will show >50% would purchase a 406 MHz distress beacon at a price point of $200-300.
Sales of ACR’s existing PLB will increase if marketed as a consumer product.
Competitor entry will be limited by regulatory exclusivity and high cost of entry.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: Regulatory mandate (FCC approval, NOAA registration) and the need for reliable distress signaling in remote areas create a demand for a compliant consumer device that can be integrated into existing safety protocols.
T2.how_value_is_captured: ACR can sell a specialized, high‑margin distress beacon through marine distributors and safety equipment retailers, leveraging its existing B2B relationships to capture value from a new consumer segment.
assumptions: Regulatory bodies will continue to enforce compliance requirements for consumer devices.
Commercial operators will prioritize safety over cost in a regulatory environment.
Distribution channels serving marine and safety markets can reach the target audience.
predictions: A survey of marine operators and safety professionals will show >40% would purchase a 406 MHz distress beacon at a price point of $500-800.
Sales of ACR’s existing PLB will increase if marketed as a compliance‑grade consumer product.
Competitor entry will be limited by the high regulatory barrier and the need for specialized integration.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Outdoor Recreation vs. Commercial Marine
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Outdoor Recreation Group (recruited from outdoor enthusiast forums and outdoor retailer mailing lists) and Commercial Marine Group (recruited from marine industry newsletters and safety equipment distributors). Each participant views a product description of a 406 MHz PLB (specifying its distress capability, FCC approval, and price point of €300) and is asked: "Would you purchase this device for personal use?" (Yes/No).
X1.sample: 200 participants (100 per group). Outdoor Recreation Group: 100 registered outdoor enthusiasts (hikers, paddlers, climbers) who have participated in activities where emergency response is limited. Commercial Marine Group: 100 professionals (marine operators, crew members, search and rescue personnel) who work in environments where reliable distress signaling is required.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (Yes) and willingness to pay (WTP) measured as a percentage of participants who would buy the device at the given price point.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor Recreation Group will show a purchase intent rate ≥50% and a WTP ≥50% at €300; Commercial Marine Group will show a purchase intent rate <30% and a WTP <50% at €300.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Commercial Marine Group will show a purchase intent rate ≥40% and a WTP ≥50% at €300; Outdoor Recreation Group will show a purchase intent rate <30% and a WTP <50% at €300.

X1.decision_rule: If Outdoor Recreation Group purchase intent ≥50% AND WTP ≥50% at €300, proceed with consumer proposition for outdoor recreation. If Commercial Marine Group purchase intent ≥40% AND WTP ≥50% at €300, proceed with compliance-grade consumer proposition for marine operators. If neither group meets both thresholds, recommend no expansion.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer demand, price sensitivity, or adoption behavior for outdoor recreation users. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed consumer preference survey (Test X1) to validate demand before committing resources. If the survey meets the thresholds, proceed with a limited launch of a consumer-branded distress beacon; otherwise, maintain the existing B2B/B2G focus.
final.target_customer: Outdoor recreation participants (hikers, paddlers, climbers) who engage in activities where emergency response is limited and are willing to pay a premium for reliable distress signaling.
final.value_proposition: A premium-priced, easy-to-use 406 MHz distress beacon that leverages ACR’s existing PLB technology to provide reliable distress signaling in remote environments, sold through outdoor retailers and online channels.
final.next_action: Run the consumer preference survey (Test X1) within the 12‑week budget of €15,000 to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a €300 device.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand and price sensitivity. The survey will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the survey shows <30% purchase intent or <50% willingness to pay at €300 for the outdoor group, we would abandon T1 and focus on the marine/commercial segment (supporting T2).
If the survey shows ≥50% purchase intent and ≥50% willingness to pay for the outdoor group, we would proceed with a consumer launch based on T1.
If new evidence emerges showing strong demand from marine operators or personal safety professionals, we would reconsider T2.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Outdoor Recreation vs. Commercial Marine
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Outdoor Recreation Group (recruited from outdoor enthusiast forums and outdoor retailer mailing lists) and Commercial Marine Group (recruited from marine industry newsletters and safety equipment distributors). Each participant views a product description of a 406 MHz PLB (specifying its distress capability, FCC approval, and price point of €300) and is asked: "Would you purchase this device for personal use?" (Yes/No).
arguments.sample: 200 participants (100 per group). Outdoor Recreation Group: 100 registered outdoor enthusiasts (hikers, paddlers, climbers) who have participated in activities where emergency response is limited. Commercial Marine Group: 100 professionals (marine operators, crew members, search and rescue personnel) who work in environments where reliable distress signaling is required.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (Yes) and willingness to pay (WTP) measured as a percentage of participants who would buy the device at the given price point.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Outdoor Recreation Group will show a purchase intent rate ≥50% and a WTP ≥50% at €300; Commercial Marine Group will show a purchase intent rate <30% and a WTP <50% at €300.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Commercial Marine Group will show a purchase intent rate ≥40% and a WTP ≥50% at €300; Outdoor Recreation Group will show a purchase intent rate <30% and a WTP <50% at €300.

arguments.decision_rule: If Outdoor Recreation Group purchase intent ≥50% AND WTP ≥50% at €300, proceed with consumer proposition for outdoor recreation. If Commercial Marine Group purchase intent ≥40% AND WTP ≥50% at €300, proceed with compliance-grade consumer proposition for marine operators. If neither group meets both thresholds, recommend no expansion.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed consumer preference survey (Test X1) to validate demand before committing resources. If the survey meets the thresholds, proceed with a limited launch of a consumer-branded distress beacon; otherwise, maintain the existing B2B/B2G focus.

arguments.target_customer: Outdoor recreation participants (hikers, paddlers, climbers) who engage in activities where emergency response is limited and are willing to pay a premium for reliable distress signaling.
arguments.value_proposition: A premium-priced, easy-to-use 406 MHz distress beacon that leverages ACR’s existing PLB technology to provide reliable distress signaling in remote environments, sold through outdoor retailers and online channels.
arguments.next_action: Run the consumer preference survey (Test X1) within the 12‑week budget of €15,000 to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a €300 device.
arguments.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand and price sensitivity. The survey will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the survey shows <30% purchase intent or <50% willingness to pay at €300 for the outdoor group, we would abandon T1 and focus on the marine/commercial segment (supporting T2).
If the survey shows ≥50% purchase intent and ≥50% willingness to pay for the outdoor group, we would proceed with a consumer launch based on T1.
If new evidence emerges showing strong demand from marine operators or personal safety professionals, we would reconsider T2.

position.recommendation: Invest in a limited pilot of a safety‑focused outdoor recreation distress beacon, using the proposed 12‑week online survey test to validate purchase intent under safety messaging versus lifestyle messaging. If the pilot shows safety‑focused intent meeting the decision threshold, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer product; otherwise, reconsider expansion or license the technology to third parties. The test’s

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, based on evidence available in late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Uncertainty about ACR’s current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer distress beacons.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, competitive landscape, and value capture for ACR.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product (e.g., portable emergency distress beacon for outdoor recreation) using the 406 MHz technology.
2) Expand the existing B2B/B2G product line into new segments (e.g., commercial marine, personal safety) without a new consumer proposition.
3) No expansion – maintain current product portfolio and focus resources on existing markets.
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third parties for consumer applications, capturing value through royalties.
5) Form a partnership with outdoor/recreational brands to co‑brand a consumer distress beacon, leveraging existing distribution channels.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: If ACR positions the beacon as a required safety device for high‑risk activities, users will purchase it to meet regulatory requirements and reduce perceived risk.
T1.how_value_is_captured: ACR can charge premium prices for a safety‑certified product and sell through outdoor retailers and online channels, capturing value through direct sales and potential licensing of the technology.
assumptions: Outdoor recreation market in 2002 is large enough to support a differentiated product.
Regulators enforce 406 MHz registration requirements for outdoor activities.
Consumers are willing to pay a premium for safety‑certified emergency devices.
predictions: Surveyed outdoor recreation participants will indicate intent to purchase a 406 MHz distress beacon when presented with safety‑focused messaging.
Sales of ACR’s outdoor‑focused beacon will exceed sales of its existing B2B/B2G products in the same period.

X1.name: Outdoor Recreation Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two messaging conditions: (A) Safety‑focused messaging emphasizing regulatory compliance and emergency reliability; (B) Lifestyle‑focused messaging emphasizing status, exclusivity, and extreme‑activity signaling. Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7‑point scale (1‑“Very unlikely” to 7‑“Very likely”).
X1.sample: 200 outdoor recreation enthusiasts recruited via outdoor forums and social media, balanced across age, gender, and experience levels.
X1.measure: Average purchase intent score for each condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent under safety‑focused messaging than under lifestyle‑focused messaging.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent under lifestyle‑focused messaging than under safety‑focused messaging.

X1.decision_rule: If safety‑focused mean ≥ 5.5 and lifestyle‑focused mean ≤ 4.5, conclude T1 is better supported. If lifestyle‑focused mean ≥ 5.5 and safety‑focused mean ≤ 4.5, conclude T2 is better supported. If both means ≥ 5.5, both theories remain uncertain.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer demand, regulatory compliance, or outdoor recreation adoption. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a limited pilot of a safety‑focused outdoor recreation distress beacon, using the proposed 12‑week online survey test to validate purchase intent under safety messaging versus lifestyle messaging. If the pilot shows safety‑focused intent meeting the decision threshold, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer product; otherwise, reconsider expansion or license the technology to third parties.
final.target_customer: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts (hikers, climbers, campers) who value emergency reliability and regulatory compliance.
final.value_proposition: A 406 MHz distress beacon marketed as a safety‑critical tool for remote travel, meeting regulatory requirements and reducing perceived risk, sold through outdoor retailers and online channels at a premium price.
final.next_action: Run the proposed 12‑week online survey test with 200 outdoor recreation participants, allocate €15,000 budget, and analyze results against the decision threshold (safety‑focused mean ≥ 5.5, lifestyle‑focused mean ≤ 4.5).
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand and willingness to pay for a 406 MHz distress beacon in 2002.
would_change_if: If the pilot shows lifestyle‑focused messaging generating higher purchase intent than safety messaging, we would shift focus to a lifestyle‑branded product.
If neither messaging meets the decision threshold, we would recommend no expansion and explore licensing the technology to third parties.

arguments.sample: 200 outdoor recreation enthusiasts recruited via outdoor forums and social media, balanced across age, gender, and experience levels.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify current reach to individual buyers from public sources.
Evidence must address demand, feasibility, and value capture for a consumer proposition.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale farming, home gardening, or recreational use) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers directly without a differentiated proposition (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer sales or new dealer partnerships).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on the current B2B dealer model and existing product lines.
4) License tractor technology to third parties for consumer applications (e.g., automotive or recreational vehicle manufacturers).

T1.claim: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they perceive them as a practical, inexpensive tool for multiple tasks, and they can purchase them through existing dealer networks without requiring new channels.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners gain a versatile, low‑cost device for yard work; Deere benefits by selling through its existing dealer network, avoiding new distribution costs.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Rapidly increasing small‑garden households need a tool that can handle various chores; the tractor's low price and ease of use make it attractive compared to manual tools.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere captures value by selling tractors through its existing dealer network, leveraging existing relationships and avoiding the need for new retail channels.
assumptions: Small‑garden households in 1962 have sufficient disposable income to afford a lawn tractor.
Deere's dealer network is willing and able to stock and sell lawn tractors.
Consumers trust Deere's brand for agricultural equipment and will extend that trust to lawn and garden products.
predictions: If Deere introduces a lawn and garden tractor, dealers will order sufficient units to meet demand within 12 weeks.
Consumer surveys from 1962 will show that at least 30% of households with small gardens have considered purchasing a lawn tractor.
Sales of lawn and garden equipment will increase overall dealer revenue by at least 5% in the first year.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they perceive them as a practical, inexpensive tool for multiple tasks, and they can purchase them through existing dealer networks without requiring new channels.

T2.claim: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they represent a new, convenient way to perform yard work, and they are willing to purchase through existing dealer networks if the product is positioned as a consumer convenience rather than a purely agricultural tool.
T2.who_benefits: Homeowners gain a time‑saving, convenient device for yard work; Deere benefits by selling through its existing dealer network, leveraging existing relationships and avoiding new retail channels.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Growing suburban populations and increasing leisure time create demand for quick, easy yard work solutions; a tractor that can handle multiple tasks without manual effort is perceived as a modern convenience.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere captures value by selling tractors through its existing dealer network, positioning the product as a consumer convenience rather than a farm tool, and earning premium pricing for a differentiated offering.
assumptions: Suburban households in 1962 have sufficient disposable income to afford a lawn tractor priced above basic tools.
Deere can market the tractor as a consumer convenience without damaging its agricultural brand.
Dealers will stock the tractor if it is presented as a modern, time‑saving product.
predictions: If Deere introduces a lawn and garden tractor marketed as a consumer convenience, dealers will order sufficient units to meet demand within 12 weeks.
Consumer surveys from 1962 will show that at least 25% of households with small gardens have considered purchasing a lawn tractor primarily for convenience.

arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are shown a product description of a lawn tractor (specifications, price, and a brief description emphasizing either time‑saving convenience or modern lifestyle status). arguments.sample: 500 U.S. homeowners aged 30‑65, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and region. Participants must have owned a lawn or garden tool in the past year.
arguments.measure: Percentage of participants who select "convenience/time‑saving" as the primary benefit (T1) and percentage who select "status/modern lifestyle" as the primary benefit (T2). Secondary measure: average premium willingness‑to‑pay (WTP) in dollars.

arguments.decision_rule: If the observed percentage selecting "convenience/time‑saving" is at least 60% and WTP is below 20% premium, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition focused on time‑saving convenience.
